levels.title: Narrative Sabotage
levels.body: Intentionally fabricates or distorts a sequence of events to scapegoat others or hide critical systemic failures. Example: The Revisionist — "The project failed because the Marketing team ignored the brief from day one. I warned them, but they chose to fail." (The subject uses a false 'villain' narrative to hide their own lack of oversight).

levels.title: Toxic Framing
levels.body: Uses stories to create "Us vs. Them" dynamics, purposefully demoralizing initiatives or reinforcing harmful hierarchies. Example: The Divider — "Remember when the 'suits' upstairs tried this in 2018 and it blew up in our faces? This new plan is just history repeating itself."

levels.title: The Dead-End Loop
levels.body: Starts a story but loses the thread or fails to provide a resolution, leaving the audience with unresolved cognitive tension. Example: The Trail-Follower — "So, I was talking to the client, and they mentioned their dog... anyway, the dog was a lab... wait, what was I saying about the contract? I guess it's fine."

levels.title: Narrative Chaos
levels.body: Presents information without any chronological or logical sequence, making it impossible for the listener to follow the "thread." Example: The Shuffled Deck — "We need to fix the bug. Last week we had a meeting. The CEO wants growth. I sent an email on Tuesday. Does that make sense?"

levels.title: The Data Dump
levels.body: Provides a list of facts or events without a "Why" or any emotional connection, failing to engage the listener's memory. Example: The Human Spreadsheet — "Event A happened at 9 AM. Event B happened at 10 AM. Event C followed. End of report."

levels.title: The Sequence Starter
levels.body: Follows a basic chronological arc (Once upon a time... Every day... Until one day...) that allows for predictable clarity. Example: The Chronological Narrator — "Once we had a stable market. Every day we sold X. Until one day, a new competitor arrived. Because of that, we had to change. Finally, we recovered."

levels.title: Contextual Grounding
levels.body: Establishes the "Who, What, and Where" clearly before diving into the details of the story. Example: The Scene Setter — "Before I tell you about the bug, you need to understand that our team was working 60-hour weeks in the middle of a server migration. That is the world where this mistake happened."

levels.title: The Hook & Payoff
levels.body: Uses an engaging opening to grab attention and ensures the story ends with a clear, valuable "Moral" or "Lesson." Example: The Engagement Builder — "Imagine losing half million in sixty seconds. That was our reality last Tuesday. Here is the story of how we found the leak and why it will never happen again."

levels.title: Descriptive Vibrancy
levels.body: Uses "Mental Images" and specific details to make a story more concrete and less abstract. Example: The Painter — "The client wasn't just 'unhappy.' They were sitting in a silent office with ten broken monitors, staring at a blank screen. That is the urgency we are dealing with."

levels.title: Narrative Pacing
levels.body: Consciously alternates between tension and relief, using pauses to let important narrative moments "sink in." Example: The Rhythm-Keeper — "We pushed the code. We waited. (Long pause). And then, for the first time in three years... the system held."

levels.title: The Hero's Journey (Self-Growth)
levels.body: Frames a professional challenge as a personal "Quest," where the struggle leads to a tangible gain in knowledge or skill. Example: The Quest Narrator — "I thought I knew everything about sales. Then I met this client who challenged every assumption I had. That 'failure' was the mentor I didn't know I needed."

levels.title: Humanizing Data
levels.body: Wraps complex statistics or technical themes in a personal story to make them relatable to a non-expert audience. Example: The Data Translator — "This 2% increase in latency isn't just a number. It's the story of a mother trying to pay her bills whose app crashes right at the finish line. That is who we are fixing this for."

levels.title: The Vulnerable Bridge
levels.body: Shares authentic "Failure Stories" to lower the team's defensiveness and normalize learning from mistakes. Example: The Humanizer — "I once deleted a production database early in my career. I'm telling you this because I want you to know that mistakes are part of our story, not the end of it."

levels.title: The Analogous Leap
levels.body: Uses sophisticated metaphors to simplify high-complexity organizational shifts. Example: The Metaphor Architect — "Our current strategy is like a heavy anchor. It kept us safe during the storm, but now the sun is out and we need to cut the rope if we want to actually sail."

levels.title: Resistance Reframing
levels.body: Uses storytelling to address objections pre-emptively, turning a "Threat" narrative into a "Challenge" narrative. Example: The Perspective Shifter — "I know the new AI tool feels like a replacement. But think of it as moving from being the person digging the hole to the person driving the excavator. We are just getting more power."

levels.title: The Strategic Pivot Story
levels.body: Translates a dry strategic plan into a compelling "Future Vision" narrative that makes change feel desirable. Example: The Vision Caster — "We aren't just 'cutting costs.' We are clearing the overgrown forest so we can finally see the path to the mountain. This is the beginning of our new chapter."

levels.title: The Mindset Catalyst
levels.body: Uses a story to trigger a permanent shift in how a team perceives its own capacity or mission. Example: The Belief-Builder — "We used to think we were a 'Support' team. But after seeing how you saved that account, it's clear we are actually the 'Retention Engine' of this company. Our story changed today."

levels.title: The Viral Narrative
levels.body: Crafts stories so simple and resonant that they are spontaneously repeated by others, becoming part of the "Team Folklore." Example: The Myth-Maker — The subject shares a story of extreme customer service that becomes "The Legend of the Friday Night Fix," which every new hire hears on day one.

levels.title: The Strategy-as-Story
levels.body: Communicates massive organizational transformations as a cohesive narrative that makes 1,000 moving parts feel like one logical journey. Example: The Master Architect — "During the M&A, I didn't give them a chart. I told them the story of two rivers joining to create a force that could reach the ocean. The logic was in the flow, not the spreadsheet."

levels.title: The Existential Reset
levels.body: Uses a "Watershed Story" to help an organization "Unlearn" its past success and pivot to a new identity during an existential crisis. Example: The Paradigm Shifter — "Our old success is a ghost haunting our future. It's time to bury the ghost so we can become the pioneers we were 20 years ago. Let's write the first page of the new book."

levels.title: The Cultural Mythos (Legacy)
levels.body: Defines the organization's enduring purpose through a master narrative that survives the leader's presence and dictates behavior for decades. Example: The Identity Architect — The subject's story about "Why we exist" becomes the foundational "Founding Myth" that guides every strategic decision, M&A, and hire for the next generation of the company.
